analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to offer shared community solar programs open to all ratepayers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2025 by Rep. Castor and 12 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees and has had no further action or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 utility law (PURPA) to require every electric utility except Tribal utilities to offer a community solar program, meaning customers could buy into a shared solar farm and have the power it generates credited against their electric bill. It requires state regulators to formally consider this rule within set deadlines, directs the Energy Department to run a program to expand community solar access with technical help and financing, and extends federal utility contracts to 30 years so agencies can participate too. The federal role is a nudge: states must hold hearings and make a determination, but they can still decline to adopt the standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, apartment dwellers, and people whose roofs are shaded or otherwise unsuitable for panels — especially low- and moderate-income households — could subscribe to a shared solar project and get bill credits, something rooftop solar can't offer them. Community solar developers and, where they choose to participate, electric utilities gain a larger customer base.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and low-income households without rooftops

how_it_helps.text: Amends PURPA to require every non-Tribal electric utility to offer a community solar program with 'equitable and demonstrable access' for all ratepayers, including low-income ratepayers.

Requires each state regulator and nonregulated utility to begin considering the community solar standard within one year and complete that consideration within two years; states that already adopted a comparable standard are exempt.

Directs the Energy Department to establish a program to expand community solar access, aligned with existing low-income programs, including technical assistance to state, local, and Tribal governments and data support to help finance projects.

Expands DOE's existing grant, loan, and financing programs to include community solar, and extends federal contracts for public utility services from their current limit to 30 years so federal facilities can participate long-term.

Requires each community solar program to include a mechanism allowing utilities, non-utilities, and other entities to take ownership stakes in the solar facilities, aimed at delivering customer benefits and limiting market concentration.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities bear the cost of setting up and administering community solar programs, and some of that cost can flow to ratepayers. Subscription middleman companies can also take a share of the benefit if state-set credit rates leave a spread.

drawbacks.text: The federal rule is a consideration standard, not a mandate: states must hold hearings and make a determination but can still decline to adopt community solar, so no utility anywhere is guaranteed to offer it.

The value of the bill credit each subscriber gets is decided in state utility proceedings; if states set it low, third-party subscription companies can capture part of the benefit and customers see little savings.
Utilities face new administrative and program costs, which can be recovered through rates paid by all customers, including those who never subscribe.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for the roughly half of households that cannot host rooftop panels — it gives them a way to buy solar and cut bills. But the bill is a lever, not a switch: it forces consideration rather than adoption, and whether customers actually save depends entirely on how state regulators value the bill credits and whether subscription middlemen pass the value through. Costs to utilities are modest relative to the potential access, but poorly designed state programs could deliver little to subscribers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late June 2025 and sent to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the bill in the House on June 26, 2025, joined by 10 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
All 12 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
No committee markup, floor vote, or other action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has won or lost anything — the bill has not moved past committee referral, which means utilities and their regulators face no new obligations yet and community solar developers have no new federal backing yet.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Solar Consumer Choice Act of 2025 in the House.

for.name: 12 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill; all are Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no opposition is on the record, but all 13 supporters in the House are Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored.

industries.industry: Community solar developers and subscription companies
industries.note: A federal push plus a PURPA standard requiring every utility to consider a community solar program would greatly expand the pool of potential subscribers. The bill tries to keep the benefit with customers by requiring programs to allow utility and subscriber ownership and to mitigate market concentration, but if states set low bill-credit rates, middleman companies can still take a cut.

Utilities would have to offer a community solar program open equitably to all ratepayers and absorb new administrative costs. But the bill lets utilities own community solar facilities themselves, so they can also gain a new revenue line from the same customers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits without action in a Republican-controlled House with no Republican cosponsors, and the large majority of bills referred to committee never reach the floor. Unless it picks up bipartisan support or moves through Energy and Commerce quickly, it is likely to expire without a vote at the end of this Congress.
